topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 3-D shapes
topic.description: Recognise and name common 3-D shapes (cubes, cuboids, pyramids, spheres, cylinders, cones)
evidence: Name a cube, sphere, cylinder, and cone when shown them
Identify 3-D shapes in the environment (e.g. a tin is a cylinder)
Recognise a cuboid and a pyramid among a set of solid shapes
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} name common 3-D shapes they find around them — like a tin of beans (cylinder), a ball (sphere), or a dice (cube)?

pedagogy.summary: Naming solids builds on the same feature-versus-prototype idea as 2-D shapes, with an extra hurdle: children readily DISCRIMINATE solids (they can tell a ball from a block, a sphere from a cube) and pick up the names quickly, but that naming is superficial — the real learning is beginning to analyse solids by their properties (flat vs curved surfaces, whether they roll, corners) and, above all, NOT confusing a solid with its flat 2-D 'cousin'. The signature error is applying a flat shape name to a solid object — a ball or coin called a 'circle', a box called a 'square'. It is taught best with real objects children HANDLE, anchored to everyday twins (a ball is a sphere, a can a cylinder, a cereal box a cuboid), using a simple 'can you pick it up?' test to separate solid from flat.
bestPractices: Use real, handled objects — children hold, turn and feel solids; the perception of solidity (you can pick it up and turn it over) is what marks a 3-D shape off from a flat 2-D one.

Anchor each solid to an everyday twin (ball = sphere, tin/can = cylinder, cereal box = cuboid, party hat = cone, dice = cube) and accept informal 'ball-shaped' language while modelling the formal name.
Use the 'can you pick it up / hold it?' test to separate solid (3-D) from flat (2-D), directly countering the coin-is-a-circle error.
Draw attention to properties in informal terms — flat versus curved surfaces, whether it rolls, how many corners — e.g. choosing cylinders for wheels 'because they roll'.
Vary the examples (cuboids of many proportions, cones and cylinders of different sizes) so a solid is recognised by its properties, not by one remembered prototype.
keyRepresentations: Real solids to handle, each beside its everyday-object twin
'Can you pick it up?' flat-versus-solid sort (2-D card vs 3-D object)
Feely-bag / guess-by-touch, justifying from properties
Rolls / doesn't-roll and flat / curved surface cues
commonMisconceptions: Calls a solid by its flat 2-D name, or treats a solid object as a flat shape: a ball or coin is a 'circle', a box is a 'square' (the coin-is-2D error).
Recognises only the prototype (a party-hat cone, a dice-sized cube) and hesitates on unusual proportions such as a tall thin cuboid or a wide flat cylinder.
Names by the object rather than the shape ('it's a tin') without generalising to other cylinders.
Can point to or discriminate solids correctly yet know no defining property — perception without analysis.

learn.summary: Young children (about 4–6) quickly tell solids apart and pick up their names, but that naming is often superficial. The real learning is beginning to analyse solids by properties (flat vs curved surfaces, whether they roll, corners) and, crucially, not confusing a solid with its flat 2-D 'cousin' — the signature error of calling a ball or coin a 'circle' or a box a 'square'. Best taught with real objects children handle, anchored to everyday twins (ball = sphere, can = cylinder, cereal box = cuboid, party hat = cone, dice = cube). To separate a solid from a flat shape, focus on whether the object is solid with bulk on every side (round all over, or thickness all the way round) rather than simply whether it can be picked up — a flat card drawn with a circle can also be picked up and has slight thickness, yet it represents an ideal flat 2-D shape, while a round coin is a solid short cylinder. Screen or 3-D models can rehearse rotation and the circle/cylinder insight but sit alongside, not instead of, a basket of real objects.

activities.title: Handle, turn and name real solids
feedback: If a child calls the ball or coin a 'circle', contrast a flat drawing of a circle with the ball itself: the ball is round and solid on every side, the drawing is flat. Turn the object to show it is solid all over, then re-anchor: ball = sphere.
If a coin or tin is placed with the flat shapes, show it has bulk and thickness all the way round, so it is a solid (a round coin is a short cylinder), unlike the flat shape drawn on the card.
Accept informal 'ball-shaped' or 'tin-shaped' language, then model the formal name alongside it.
activities.rationale: What marks a 3-D shape off from a flat one is being solid with bulk on every side, which this age grasps by handling and turning real objects. Pick-up-ability is not a reliable cue because a flat card can also be lifted and has slight thickness, so attend to solidity and to the shape represented. Anchoring to everyday twins and noticing thickness all round directly counters the coin-is-flat error.
sourceClaims: Children easily discriminate 3-D solids (e.g. a rectangular prism like a book from a sphere like a ball, or a sphere from a cube) and may know the names, but the ability to discriminate is only 'seeing that they look different' — they may know no defining property; learning names is easy and superficial, so the goal is analysing solids by properties, best served by handling and by teaching properties, not labels alone.

A documented misconception is that children incorrectly say items like coins are 2-D/flat shapes; teachers should explain a coin is a 3-D shape (a cylinder) because it has height and is solid, using the test that 2-D shapes are flat and cannot be picked up while 3-D shapes are solid and can be held, and anchoring solids to everyday objects (a ball is a sphere, a cereal box a cuboid, a can a cylinder).

NCETM Early Years guidance treats shape as spatial reasoning about properties, recommends drawing attention to 3-D properties (edges, faces, vertices, curvedness), handling real objects and choosing them for a purpose (cylinders as wheels because they roll), validating informal 'ball-shaped' language, and linking 2-D faces to 3-D solids.
learnerActions: Pick up, turn and feel each real solid (cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, cuboid, pyramid), saying what you notice.
Match each solid to its everyday twin: ball = sphere, tin/can = cylinder, cereal box = cuboid, party hat = cone, dice = cube.

Compare a solid object with a flat card that has a circle or a square drawn on it: notice the solid has bulk on every side (it is round all over, or has thickness all the way round), while the card pictures a flat shape. Sort them into 'flat shape' and 'solid' piles, putting a coin and a tin with the SOLIDS because they are solid all round (a round coin is a short cylinder). Note the approximation: a real card is not perfectly flat — it has slight thickness — but it stands for an ideal flat 2-D shape.
Describe each solid informally: does it have flat or curved surfaces? does it roll? how many corners?
activities.intendedInsight: A 3-D shape is a solid object with bulk on every side; it is distinct from a flat 2-D shape even when it looks round or square. A circle or square drawn on a card is just a picture of a flat shape, while a coin or ball is solid all round. Names should attach to properties, not just to one object.

activities.title: The circle-on-the-cylinder discovery
feedback: If the child still says the cylinder 'is a circle', show the curved middle: 'The circle is only one face; the whole thing is solid all round, it rolls, and we call it a cylinder.'
Ask 'Why does the ball roll but the box doesn't?' to draw out curved vs flat surfaces.
activities.rationale: The circle-vs-cylinder confusion is the deepest form of the 2-D-name-for-a-solid error; letting the child see a cylinder's flat circular ends together with its curved rolling surface gives a concrete counterexample. A rotatable model can make hidden faces and rolling visible, but a real tin shows the same features by hand.
sourceClaims: A documented misconception is that children incorrectly say items like coins are 2-D/flat shapes; teachers should explain a coin is a 3-D shape (a cylinder) because it has height and is solid, using the test that 2-D shapes are flat and cannot be picked up while 3-D shapes are solid and can be held, and anchoring solids to everyday objects (a ball is a sphere, a cereal box a cuboid, a can a cylinder).

NCETM Early Years guidance treats shape as spatial reasoning about properties, recommends drawing attention to 3-D properties (edges, faces, vertices, curvedness), handling real objects and choosing them for a purpose (cylinders as wheels because they roll), validating informal 'ball-shaped' language, and linking 2-D faces to 3-D solids.
learnerActions: Spin or roll a real cylinder (a tin) and look at its two ends and its middle.
Say what shape each flat end is (a circle) and describe the curved middle that lets it roll.
Answer: 'Is the WHOLE thing a circle, or does it just have circles on it?'
If a rotatable 3-D model is available, rotate a cylinder so a flat circle appears on each end while the middle shows as a curved wrap, and tap surfaces to see them light up flat or curved.
activities.intendedInsight: A circle is just one flat face of the cylinder; the whole solid you can hold and that rolls is a cylinder. Seeing both the flat ends and the curved wrap resolves the circle/cylinder confusion.

activities.title: Beyond the prototype: find and vary
feedback: If the child names only the typical example and rejects an atypically proportioned one, present several proportions and find the shared properties together.
If the child names the solid by the object and cannot find another cylinder, ask what makes it a cylinder — draw out the circular ends, curved surface and rolling to define the class.
activities.rationale: Varying examples prevents a single prototype from standing in for the concept, and 'find another one' separates a shape concept from a single object label. Using accurate examples and non-examples with 'is it or not, and why?' reasoning builds property-based recognition.
sourceClaims: The Clements & Sarama learning-trajectories approach sequences early shape work through recogniser levels using accurate examples, non-examples ('Is it or not? — and explain why') and correct names tied to defining properties (straight sides, corners), rather than mixing non-geometric figures with shapes.

Children easily discriminate 3-D solids (e.g. a rectangular prism like a book from a sphere like a ball, or a sphere from a cube) and may know the names, but the ability to discriminate is only 'seeing that they look different' — they may know no defining property; learning names is easy and superficial, so the goal is analysing solids by properties, best served by handling and by teaching properties, not labels alone.
learnerActions: Find another object in the room shaped like a cylinder that is NOT the tin you started with.
Sort cuboids of many proportions (a tall thin one, a wide flat one) and cylinders of different sizes, naming each.
For an unusual example, explain what makes it count: a cylinder always has two flat circular ends and a curved surface and rolls; a cuboid has flat rectangular faces and corners.
Answer 'What else is shaped like this? What makes it a cylinder?' rather than naming it by the object ('it's a tin').
activities.intendedInsight: A solid is recognised by its shared properties, not by one remembered prototype or by the particular object; the class 'cylinder' includes many sizes and objects.

activities.title: Feely-bag and flat-vs-solid sort (rehearsal and check)
feedback: Instant feedback should keep property cues explicit: a tin/coin goes with the solids because it is solid with bulk all the way round (a round coin is a short cylinder); a cylinder rolls and has circular ends, while a flat circle is only a picture of a flat shape.
A screen or photo cannot convey handling and rotation, so pair this rehearsal with real objects and keep naming the properties aloud.
activities.rationale: Matching, sorting and choose-the-answer tasks rehearse the solid/flat decision and everyday-twin link with immediate feedback, and distractors built from the 2-D-name-for-a-solid error target the signature confusion. These recognition formats check and reinforce classification but do not by themselves require the child to handle and analyse objects, so they supplement the hands-on work.
sourceClaims: A documented misconception is that children incorrectly say items like coins are 2-D/flat shapes; teachers should explain a coin is a 3-D shape (a cylinder) because it has height and is solid, using the test that 2-D shapes are flat and cannot be picked up while 3-D shapes are solid and can be held, and anchoring solids to everyday objects (a ball is a sphere, a cereal box a cuboid, a can a cylinder).

The Clements & Sarama learning-trajectories approach sequences early shape work through recogniser levels using accurate examples, non-examples ('Is it or not? — and explain why') and correct names tied to defining properties (straight sides, corners), rather than mixing non-geometric figures with shapes.
learnerActions: Reach into a feely-bag, feel a solid, and guess which one it is — justifying from a property you can feel ('it's round all over, with no flat faces or corners, so it's a sphere and would roll').

Sort a mixed set of real-object photos (coin, ball, tin, box, party hat) under 'flat shape' and 'solid shape', or match each photo to its solid name; remember each photo shows a solid object even though the photo itself is flat.
Choose from options 'which of these is a cylinder?' where a plain 2-D circle is one of the choices, and say why the circle is not the cylinder.
activities.intendedInsight: The solid/flat decision and the everyday-twin link can be rehearsed quickly, with the typical error (a 2-D name or a flat classification for a solid) made explicit to be corrected.

constraints: Real, handled objects are central for this age: children should hold, turn and feel solids. Screen or 3-D-model rehearsal should sit alongside a basket of real objects, not replace it.
A flat screen or photo cannot convey handling and rotation; when used, keep property cues (rolls, bulk on every side, curved vs flat surface) explicit.

Recognition formats (matching, sorting, choose-the-answer) rehearse and check the solid/flat decision and classification but do not by themselves elicit independent handling and property analysis; use them to supplement hands-on work.
Accept informal language ('ball-shaped', 'tin-shaped') and model the formal name alongside it rather than rejecting the child's words.
A tap-to-reveal labelled scene is useful as a vocabulary reference but is static — it cannot let the child rotate a solid to see hidden faces, where the analysis lives.

Distinguish the solid from its flat face explicitly: a cylinder has circular faces but is not a circle; a round coin is a short cylinder, not a flat circle. Do not rely on 'can you pick it up?' as the definition of a solid — a flat card can also be picked up and has slight thickness; instead ask whether the object is solid with bulk on every side, and ask about the mathematical shape represented on a thin card rather than whether the physical card can be lifted. A pictured or modelled solid still represents a 3-D object even though the picture is flat.

Open in-role, pretend dialogue does not by itself elicit the hands-on handling, turning and rotation this naming task relies on at this age; spoken questioning can still draw out property talk, but it should accompany work with real solids rather than stand in for it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The Oxford Owl source phrases the method as '2-D shapes are flat and cannot be picked up while 3-D shapes can be held'. Taken literally this is unreliable, because card/photo representations can also be picked up and have slight thickness. It has been corrected throughout to a solidity/bulk cue (solid on every side; a coin is a short cylinder) and to asking about the shape represented on a thin card, while preserving the source's intent of distinguishing a solid from a flat shape.

The claim that a 3-D interactive is 'the closest digital match' and that handling/rotation can only be fully grasped in three dimensions reflects a catalog preference; it has been softened to 'rotatable models can make hidden faces and rolling visible' alongside real objects. Comparative efficacy of 3-D model vs real objects is not established by the cited sources.

Legacy fit rankings (ideal/strong/possible/poor) and product/artefact-type vocabulary were removed; the underlying pedagogical purposes were retained as separate activities, and the residual 'poor fit' wording for dialogue was reframed as a narrow affordance limitation.

probeDeeper: Can you hold a circle in your hand? Can you hold a ball? So which one is the sphere? (flat-vs-solid counter)
Find another cylinder in the room that is NOT this tin. (transfer beyond the object label)
Look at the end of this cylinder — what shape is it? Is the WHOLE thing a circle, or does it just have circles on it? (counterexample resolving circle/cylinder)
Why does the ball roll but the box doesn't? (property talk — curved versus flat surfaces)
assess.correctAnswer: Points to each solid correctly across everyday examples, finds a real cylinder in the room, says the ball is a SPHERE (a solid you can pick up and turn, round all over) not a circle, and classes the coin/tin as SOLID because you can hold it / it has thickness — justifying by a property, not by resemblance to a flat shape.

errorPatterns.pattern: Applies a flat 2-D name to a solid, or classes a solid object as flat: a ball or coin is a 'circle', a box is a 'square'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use the 'can you pick it up and turn it over?' test; rotate the object to show it is round/solid all over and has thickness; re-anchor to the everyday twin plus the formal name (ball = sphere).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names solids with 2-D words, or puts the coin/tin with the flat shapes; says the ball is a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Recognises only the prototype solid (a dice cube, a party-hat cone) and hesitates on unusual proportions such as a tall thin cuboid or a wide flat cylinder
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show cuboids and cylinders of many proportions; find the shared properties (a cylinder always has two flat circular ends and a curved surface, and rolls).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the typical example confidently but rejects or is unsure about an atypically-proportioned cuboid or cylinder.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names the solid by the object rather than the shape ('it's a tin') and does not generalise to other cylinders
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'what else is shaped like this? what makes it a cylinder?' — draw out the flat circular ends, curved surface and rolling to define the class.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses the object name and, asked for another cylinder, cannot find one that isn't the original object.

responseLevels.gap: Uses flat 2-D names for solids (ball = 'circle') or classes solid objects as flat, and/or names only by the object ('a tin') with no property.
responseLevels.full: Names solids across varied examples, finds them in the environment, keeps a solid distinct from its flat cousin (sphere, not circle), and justifies by a property (you can hold it / it has thickness; circular ends; it rolls) — transferring to a new object.
responseLevels.partial: Names the prototypical solids and matches everyday twins, but slips on the flat/solid distinction for a borderline object (a coin) or on an atypically-proportioned solid, or names correctly without giving any property.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Put out real solids (cube, sphere, cylinder, cone, cuboid, pyramid) mixed with two flat cards (a circle and a square). Say: 'Point to the sphere. Point to the cylinder. Now find something in the room shaped like a cylinder.' Then hold up the ball and ask 'Is this a circle or a sphere — how do you know?', and hold up a coin or tin and ask 'Is this a flat shape or a solid shape — how can you tell?'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who has begun to analyse says 'sphere — it's solid, round all over, I can hold it' and finds a real cylinder; a child confusing 2-D and 3-D calls the ball a 'circle' and the tin/coin 'flat'. The 'how do you know / can you pick it up' tier separates solid-property reasoning from flat-name resemblance, and 'find another cylinder' separates a shape concept from a single object label.

topic.subject: Mathematics
topic.name: 3-D shapes (age 5+)
topic.description: Analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes using informal language to describe sides, vertices, and other attributes
evidence: Count the sides and corners of a shape
Compare a triangle and a rectangle by number of sides
Describe a cube as having 'square faces' and 'corners'
topic.assessmentPrompt: Can {{name}} describe what makes two shapes different — for example, explaining that a triangle has 3 corners and 3 sides while a square has 4 of each?

pedagogy.summary: This is the step from NAMING shapes to DESCRIBING them by their parts — the van Hiele shift from the visual level (a shape is recognised by its overall look) to the descriptive/analytic level (a shape is understood by countable attributes: sides and corners of 2-D shapes; faces, edges and corners of solids). At age 5-6 the language stays informal, but the mathematical work is that children attend to component attributes rather than the holistic silhouette, and can compare two shapes by a single countable property. It is best taught with real, handleable shapes that children touch and count, comparing many varied examples so attention shifts from appearance to structure, and drawing the crucial distinction that each flat face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape.
bestPractices: Give children physical 2-D tiles and 3-D solids to hold; count sides, corners and faces by touching and MARKING each one (sticker/pen) so none is double-counted or missed.

Compare pairs of shapes on ONE countable property at a time ('which has more sides?'), deliberately varying size and orientation so children learn the property is independent of how big or which way up the shape is drawn.
Model precise-but-informal language ('this face is a square', 'this shape has 3 straight sides and 3 corners') and have children echo it while pointing.
Draw out the distinction between a flat 2-D shape and the flat FACE of a 3-D solid — each face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape; use the 'can you pick it up? is it flat or solid?' test.
Use atypical, 'wonky' exemplars (long thin triangles, tilted rectangles) and non-examples to break reliance on a single prototypical picture.
keyRepresentations: Handleable wooden/plastic 2-D shape tiles and 3-D solids (cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone)
Geoboards / pin-boards for making and counting the sides of a 2-D shape
Feely-bag: describe a solid by touch alone (forces attention to faces/edges/corners, not colour)
A 'peel-off' image of a solid whose faces lift away as separate 2-D shapes
commonMisconceptions: Judges a shape by its overall look or size rather than counting its sides/corners (the bigger-drawn shape 'has more').
Counts only the sides/corners/faces that are visible in a picture or facing them, missing the hidden ones.
Uses everyday words loosely — 'corner' and 'side' blur the difference between a solid's face, edge and vertex.
Treats a 3-D solid as if it were the 2-D shape of one of its faces (calls a cube 'a square').

learn.summary: Help 5-6 year olds move from naming shapes by their overall look to describing them by countable parts: sides and corners for flat (2-D) shapes; flat faces, edges and corners for solids (3-D). The central work is attending to component attributes rather than the holistic silhouette, comparing two shapes on a single countable property, and grasping that each flat face of a solid is itself a 2-D shape. Best taught with real, handleable shapes children touch and count, with varied examples so attention shifts from appearance to structure. Corner/face counting is clearest with flat-faced solids such as cubes and cuboids; curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) are described by their curved surfaces. On-screen rotatable models may add value by exposing hidden back features and peeling faces, but complement rather than replace physical handling.

activities.title: Count by touching and marking every part
feedback: If a child gives a cube 4 corners or 3 faces (only the ones facing them), hand them the solid to turn and count by touch, marking each corner as it is counted; then recount from a different face to confirm the total of 8 corners is stable.
Praise counting that tracks hidden parts: 'You turned it to find the corners round the back — that's how we know there are 8.'
activities.rationale: Marking each part as it is counted prevents double-counting and omission; recounting from a new starting point builds confidence that the count is a property of the shape, not of the view. Physical handling lets children find hidden faces/corners that a single picture conceals. Keeping the corner/face count to polyhedra avoids the ill-defined case of counting 'faces' or 'corners' on a sphere.
sourceClaims: Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.

Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.
learnerActions: Hold a physical 2-D tile to count its sides and corners, or a flat-faced solid such as a cube or cuboid to count its corners and flat faces (curved solids like a sphere, cylinder or cone have curved surfaces rather than a full set of flat faces and corners, so describe those separately).
Count each side, corner or flat face by touching it and placing a sticker or pen mark on each one as it is counted, so none is double-counted or missed.
For a flat-faced solid (cube, cuboid), turn it over and count again from a different starting face to check the total stays the same.
activities.intendedInsight: A shape's number of sides/corners/flat faces is found by systematically counting all of them, including the ones round the back, not by guessing from the front view.

activities.title: Compare two shapes on one countable property
feedback: If a child picks the larger triangle as having 'more sides' because it is bigger, count each side together by touching and marking; the rectangle's 4 sides against the triangle's 3 make counting win over size.
Reinforce: 'The triangle is bigger, but the rectangle has more sides — 4 against 3. We counted them.'
activities.rationale: Deliberately drawing the triangle larger than the rectangle sets size and side-count in conflict, forcing children to rely on counting. Varying size and orientation across many examples teaches that the property does not depend on how big or which way up a shape is drawn.
sourceClaims: Common early-years errors: children treat only regular triangles/brick-like rectangles as shapes (shape defined by its typical image) and only accept squares with a horizontal base (defined by orientation); the remedy is to attend to properties (sides/corners for 2-D; edges/faces/vertices for 3-D), handle real objects, and use varied orientations, sizes and materials.
learnerActions: Look at a triangle drawn large and a rectangle drawn small, placed side by side.
Decide which has more sides, and count each side by touching and marking it.
Say which has more sides and how you know, using the count rather than the size.
activities.intendedInsight: Which shape has more sides is decided by counting, not by which is drawn bigger: the count is independent of size and orientation.

activities.title: Each face is a 2-D shape; flat vs solid
feedback: If a child names the solid by a 2-D face ('it's a square'), place a single thin tile next to the cube and talk about how the tile is flat (one 2-D shape) while the cube has depth with six square faces; name each square as one of the six faces, not the whole solid.
Affirm precise-but-informal language: 'This face is a square, and the cube has six of them.'
activities.rationale: Naming each face as a 2-D shape ON the solid, while contrasting a flat tile (one 2-D shape) with the solid's depth and six faces, targets the 2-D-name-for-a-solid confusion directly. Ask children about the mathematical shape represented; a physical tile or card has slight thickness and can be picked up, so 'can you pick it up?' is not a reliable flat-vs-solid test and is avoided here.
sourceClaims: Children often name a solid by a 2-D shape (e.g. a coin called a 'circle'); the flat-vs-solid 'can you pick it up?' test and everyday twins (ball=sphere, box=cuboid, can=cylinder) help separate a 3-D object from a 2-D shape.

Each face of a 3-D shape is a 2-D shape; an edge is the straight line where two faces meet and a vertex is the corner where edges meet; handling and manipulating solids while looking at images helps children count faces, edges and vertices.
learnerActions: Point to one face of a cube and name its 2-D shape ('this face is a square').
Check whether all the faces are the same 2-D shape.

Compare a single thin tile with the whole cube: the tile is almost flat and shows one 2-D shape, while the cube has depth and six flat faces. Note that a real tile or card has a little thickness but stands for an ideal flat shape, so talk about the shape it represents rather than whether you can pick it up.
Match everyday objects to solids and, where they have them, their flat faces (ball = sphere, no flat faces; box = cuboid, rectangle faces; can = cylinder, two circle faces and a curved surface).
activities.intendedInsight: A flat-faced solid such as a cube has flat faces that are 2-D shapes, but the solid is not the same as one of those faces: a cube is not 'a square'. Curved solids such as a sphere have curved surfaces instead of, or as well as, flat faces.

activities.title: Predict then count a cube's corners
feedback: Children who look without analysing may predict only the corners they can see from one view (for example 4 when looking straight at one face). Use the gap between the prediction and the counted 8, and their reaction to the corners 'round the back', to open a discussion about hidden features.
Encourage the realisation 'there are more round the back!' as the key moment that breaks visible-only counting.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-count structure makes the visible-only under-count visible to the child as a surprise, which motivates systematic turning-and-counting. This is a teaching use of a prediction prompt, not only an end-of-lesson check.
sourceClaims: Students represent only the visible side of a 3-D figure and under-count parts that are not directly visible, reflecting difficulty translating a 2-D representation into the full 3-D structure — grounds the hidden-feature under-count when counting corners/faces from a picture.
learnerActions: Before counting, predict out loud how many corners the cube has altogether and say the number.
Turn and mark every corner together, counting the ones round the back.
Compare the predicted number with the counted total of 8, and talk about the corners that were hidden.

constraints: Keep language informal at this age: 'corners' for vertices is acceptable; the mathematical work is attending to countable parts, not formal terminology.

A static labelled image or a scored quiz can teach vocabulary or check counts, but neither elicits the independent counting, handling and discovery of hidden features that this topic targets; use them as support or end-checks, not as the main learning experience.

Use a genuinely cube-shaped object when naming something a cube, and a cuboid for a general box.

Confine systematic corner/flat-face counting to polyhedra such as cubes and cuboids; describe curved solids (sphere, cylinder, cone) by their curved surfaces — e.g. a sphere has no flat faces, edges or corners — rather than force-fitting them to a corner/face count.

assess.poeTask: Hold up the cube. 'Predict: how many corners do you think this cube has altogether? Say your number before we count.' Most children who look without analysing predict 3 or 4 (the corners they see). Then turn and mark every corner together. assess.correctAnswer: The faces are squares; the cube has 8 corners (vertices). Crucially, the child counts systematically — turning the cube or accounting for the corners they cannot see — rather than counting only the ones facing them. Informal 'corners' for vertices is fine at this age.

pedagogy.summary: Distinguishing flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes is a foundational classification that young children find genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). It is best taught by handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space — rather than by pictures, and by giving the child a physical test ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat') alongside precise vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube). Instruction, not maturation, moves children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality (van Hiele).
bestPractices: Use real solids and flat cut-outs the child can hold and turn, not drawings — the felt three-dimensionality is what teaches the distinction.
Acknowledge the child's observation, then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle, but it is round every way and you can hold it — that is a sphere.'
Offer a child-friendly discriminator: a flat shape lies on the paper (length and width only); a solid takes up space and can be held and turned (length, width and height).
Sort mixed sets into 'flat' and 'solid', including less familiar solids (cone) and non-prototypical exemplars, and go on 'shape hunts' for solids in the room.
Teach the twin pairs explicitly — circle/sphere, square/cube, triangle/pyramid — so the flat and solid names are not confused.

Sorts by overall appearance as a whole rather than by dimensionality — groups the round ball with the round circle because both 'look round' (van Hiele visual level).
Confuses a drawing of a solid with the solid itself — treats a cube drawn on paper as 'solid' because of its name.

learn.summary: Young children (ages 5–6) distinguish flat (2-D) from solid (3-D) shapes. This is genuinely hard because everyday language mislabels solids with flat names (a ball called 'a circle', a box 'a square'). A central, curriculum-supported approach is handling real objects — holding, turning and feeling whether a shape takes up space in every direction — supported by a dimensional discriminator ('is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card?') and the explicit twin-pair vocabulary (circle/sphere, square/cube, and loosely triangle/pyramid, since a pyramid has triangle faces). A paper cut-out can itself be picked up and has a slight thickness, so 'can you pick it up?' is not the reliable test; treat the card as a stand-in for an ideal flat shape. Instruction and experience, not age alone, help move children from judging a shape by its overall look to reasoning about dimensionality.

activities.title: Hold-and-turn sort with real solids and flat cut-outs
feedback: When the child calls a solid by a flat name ('the ball is a circle'), acknowledge then press for precision: 'Yes, the ball is round like a circle — but it is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere.'

If the child groups round things together regardless of flat/solid, prompt the dimensional test: 'Is it round or thick in every direction, or is it thin and flat like the shape on a card?' Sort by that, not by how round it looks.
Reinforce correct sorts by naming the twin pair: 'Yes — the thin flat one is a circle, the one that is round in every direction is a sphere.'
activities.rationale: Handling real solids beside flat cut-outs lets the child feel three-dimensionality, which is the property being taught; sorting mixed and non-prototypical sets and naming twin pairs targets the specific confusions documented for this age. The test is framed around taking up space in every direction rather than holdability, because a paper cut-out can also be held.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.

At the van Hiele visual level, shapes are judged by their appearance and viewed as a whole, not by distinguishing parts or properties ('it's a square because it looks like one'); deliberate instruction, not maturation alone, is needed to move children to property-based (descriptive) thinking.
Kindergarten geometry requires children to identify shapes as two-dimensional (lying in a plane, 'flat') or three-dimensional ('solid').
learnerActions: Gather a mixed set the child can handle: a ball, a cube-shaped box, a pyramid, a tin, a cone, beside a paper circle, square and triangle. The paper shapes can also be picked up and have a tiny thickness, so treat each as a stand-in for the ideal flat shape it represents.
Pick up and turn each object over in your hand. Ask: is it round or thick in every direction so it takes up space (solid), or is it thin and essentially flat like the shape drawn on a card (flat)?
Sort the set into two hoops or bins labelled 'flat' and 'solid'.
Include a cone and other less familiar or non-prototypical solids, not only balls and boxes.
Go on a 'shape hunt' around the room to find more solids (a tin, a ball, a box) and say why each takes up space in every direction.
Name the twin pairs aloud as you sort: circle/sphere, square/cube, and triangle/pyramid (a pyramid has triangle faces, though its base may be a square).
activities.intendedInsight: A flat shape has length and width but (ideally) no thickness, and a paper card stands in for it; a solid takes up space in every direction (length, width and height). 'Round like a circle' is not the same as flat — a ball is round every way and takes up space all around, so it is a sphere, not a circle. (For the adult: because a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness, 'can you pick it up?' is not the real test — ask whether the shape takes up space in every direction.)

activities.title: Build a solid from flat paper (pop-up)
feedback: If the child keeps the flat name after building, point out that it now takes up space in every direction: 'This stands up and takes up space in every direction now — it is a cube, not just a square.'
Encourage counting faces to ground the solid/flat difference in something the child can touch.
activities.rationale: Constructing the solid from flat paper makes the flat-to-solid transition concrete and lets the child touch and count faces, grounding the solid name in properties the child can feel.
sourceClaims: Shown a real cube, young children named it 'square'; in the pretest 12 of the children named the square and cube both 'square' and 12 named the triangle and pyramid both 'triangle'; the cone name was unknown — children preferred the 2-D shape names their teacher had taught. The circle/sphere pair was easiest (75%). Building the solids from flat paper (pop-up) let children touch and count faces, sides and vertices and raised naming accuracy.
learnerActions: Start with a flat paper net (an unfolded pattern of joined flat shapes) and fold/assemble it into a solid (e.g. a pop-up cube or pyramid).
As the solid takes shape, touch and count its faces, edges and corners (vertices).

Compare the finished solid, which now takes up space in every direction, with the flat sheet you started from. Name the solid and the flat shapes of its faces: a cube has square faces, and a pyramid has triangle faces (a square pyramid also has a square base). The unfolded sheet (the net) is several joined shapes, not one square or triangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid takes up space in every direction and has faces you can feel and count, whereas the flat paper it came from only lies in a plane — the same name family splits into a flat word and a solid word.

activities.title: Spin-to-compare on screen (scaffold alongside handling)
feedback: If the child still calls the spun ball a circle, pair it with the physical hold: 'The one that vanished edge-on is flat; the one that stays round in every direction is a sphere.'
Note that the on-screen ball is itself a picture on a flat screen — the rotating model stands in for the real object, so pair it with a real hold-and-turn.
activities.rationale: Rotating a model shows depth from every side and a flat shape vanishing edge-on, a useful visual analogue; it is proposed as a scaffold paired with handling, not a replacement, because a flat screen does not provide the physical, tactile handling of a real object.
learnerActions: On screen, spin a circle and a ball. Watch the circle thin to a line and vanish when turned edge-on, while the ball stays round from every side.
Say why: the ideal circle has no thickness, so it disappears edge-on; the ball is round every way and never flattens — it cannot be a circle, it is a sphere.
Immediately repeat with a real paper circle and a real ball in your hand, turning each to feel that the ball is round in every direction while the card is thin.
activities.intendedInsight: An ideal flat shape has no thickness and disappears edge-on; a solid takes up space from every direction. Rotating a model shows this effect, while handling a real object additionally lets the child feel the three-dimensionality directly, so the two are paired. (A real paper circle is a thin card standing in for the zero-thickness ideal.)

constraints: Handling is central here because it lets the child feel that a ball has depth every way while a cut-out is thin. Screen activities (spin-to-compare, drag-to-sort, tap-to-reveal label cards) are offered alongside handling real objects.

A drag-to-sort flat/solid game can give feedback, but every picture on a flat screen is itself flat — this risks reinforcing appearance-based sorting, so on its own it does not elicit physical handling of real objects.
A sort or multiple-choice check can verify or practise the classification but does not itself elicit physical handling or an explanation; use it as a post-check alongside handling real objects.
Conversation alone does not let a child physically handle a shape or see it take up space; use it to prompt the child to justify a sort rather than as the sole medium.
Everyday mislabelling (ball='circle', box='square') is the main obstacle; always acknowledge the child's accurate observation ('yes, round like a circle') before correcting to the solid name.

A paper cut-out is only an approximation of an ideal flat (zero-thickness) shape: it can be picked up and has a slight thickness. So the reliable discriminator is whether the shape takes up space in every direction, not whether it can be physically held — ask the child about the mathematical shape the thin card represents.

Distinguish the drawn solid from the real one: a cube drawn on a page is flat on that page even though its name is 'cube'; contrast the drawing (whose corners you cannot grasp) with a real cube that takes up space in every direction. When naming an example a cube, use a cube-shaped object, since a generic box need not be a cube.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The source framed the 3-D interactive as the 'recommended' artefact while also stating the true lesson is physical handling; this rewrite demotes the screen rotation to an explicit scaffold paired with real objects and foregrounds the hands-on sort and pop-up build, without claiming either medium is the sole means of learning.

Original catalog text included claims that a flat screen 'cannot show' the property and that talk 'cannot convey' dimensionality. These are retained only as narrowly scoped affordances in constraints, not as universal laws; a screen model and conversation can still support learning as scaffolds.

The original row's discriminator ('can you draw it but not pick it up? then it's flat' / 'a solid can be held and turned') is an idealisation error: a paper cut-out can also be held and turned and has a slight thickness. The guidance now tests whether a shape takes up space in every direction and treats the paper card as an approximation of the ideal flat shape; this correction is applied in the activities and constraints, not only here.

pedagogy.summary: Recognising that the faces of a 3-D shape are themselves 2-D shapes (a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid) is the bridge that connects the flat and solid worlds. It is best taught by taking solids apart — unfolding or 'popping up' a solid so its faces lie flat as recognisable 2-D shapes, tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. The key idea to build is that a solid is BUILT FROM 2-D faces, and that a face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
bestPractices: Unfold or 'pop up' a solid from flat paper so children see the faces are 2-D shapes and can touch and count them (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Trace round, or dip-and-stamp, a face to print its 2-D shape — the print of a tin's end is a circle.
Name the face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) distinct from the solid's name (cylinder, pyramid, cube).
Contrast flat faces (rest flat on the table) with curved surfaces (roll), so a cylinder's curved side is not mistaken for a flat face.
Link explicitly: a cube is made of six squares; a cylinder has two circular faces — every 3-D shape is made up of 2-D shapes.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn that the flat faces of a 3-D solid are themselves 2-D shapes — a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid. A solid with only flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid, is built FROM those flat faces; some solids, such as a cylinder, also have a curved surface, which is not a flat face. The core teaching moves are taking solids apart (unfolding or popping up a solid so faces lie flat), tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid; the whole tin is a cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

pedagogy.summary: Composing 3-D shapes — stacking and combining solids to build new structures and composite shapes — develops through a well-charted progression from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION ('I know the cone goes on top'). Matched building challenges pitched one level ahead move children forward more effectively than jumping straight to the target.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to compose 3-D shapes by stacking and combining real solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres) into composite structures. The target skill is a progression: from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — knowing in advance which shape will fit ('the cone goes on top') and naming a build by its component solids and their positions. Hands-on block-building with challenges pitched one level ahead, plus prompts to predict and describe, carries children forward; because this is a procedural, construction-based goal, physical block-building is the core medium. An on-screen 3-D sandbox is an optional supplementary model that preserves stacking, balance and depth, while flat drag-and-combine and matching tasks are useful scaffolds for naming parts but do not exercise balance or anticipation.

activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids
feedback: If the child places shapes at random and names the result only afterwards, do not mark this wrong — it is an expected early level. Offer a challenge one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
If the child names only the whole ('a rocket') but not the parts, take the composite apart and name each solid together, then rebuild it, naming each shape as it goes on.

If the tower topples, look together at which faces rest on the table or on the shape below: a sphere rolls because it has no flat face, a cone balanced on its point has no flat face down, and a piece placed off-centre can tip over. So choose a flat-faced solid (a cube, prism, or cylinder on a flat face) for the base, keep each piece centred, and don't stack anything on a cone's point, rather than blaming the blocks.
Reinforce correct anticipation: when the child reaches for the cone before placing it, confirm the plan aloud ('yes — the cone fits on top of the cylinder').
activities.rationale: Composing is an action: building, balancing and anticipating are exercised by actual construction with solids, not by recognising a finished picture. The documented trajectory runs from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition to composing with anticipation and advance planning, and the curriculum asks children to compose and model shapes by building from components.
sourceClaims: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

constraints: The core objective is composing with anticipation and describing a build by its component solids and their positions — this is a procedural curriculum goal that requires actual construction, with physical block-building as the core medium, not only recognising a finished shape.

Balance depends partly on resting flat faces down: a sphere (no flat face) rolls; a cone stands steadily base-down, but it topples if balanced on its point, rolls if laid on its side, and cannot hold a block on its apex; a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face is stable on its own, although a tower can still topple if pieces are placed off-centre or it gets too tall and narrow. A fixed labelled picture can still teach part-naming as a reference, but cannot be manipulated to practise stacking or anticipation.

activities.title: Sort a real tray two ways on an 'is / is not' rule
feedback: If a child groups by colour, size or 'the pretty ones', restrict the collection to a single colour and size so appearance cannot be the criterion, forcing attention to a property.

When a placement breaks the chosen rule (e.g. a cone, which has a curved surface, dropped into 'no curved surface'), point to the mismatch and ask which property decides membership — the property, not the look.
Prompt consistency: 'Does every shape in this group follow your rule?' If membership drifts for a borderline shape, revisit the stated rule.

Watching a shape such as a triangular prism move to the other hoop when the rule changes — it has no curved surface but does have triangular faces, so it belongs in a different group under each rule — is the moment 'a sort needs one property' becomes concrete. (A cube would stay put, since it has neither a curved surface nor a triangular face.)
activities.rationale: 'Is / is not' two-set sorting with a required second re-sort of the same set targets the flexible, property-based sorting that distinguishes a child reading shapes by property from one grouping by overall look. learnerActions: Take a physical, mixed tray of handleable 2-D shapes, 3-D solids and everyday objects.

Choose ONE geometric property as the rule (e.g. 'has a curved surface / has no curved surface') and place every item into one of two sorting hoops or a labelled two-set frame. Check that the rule makes sense for every item in the tray: a flat 2-D shape such as a circle has a curved side (edge) but no curved surface, so either agree how 2-D shapes are judged or pick a rule that fits both 2-D and 3-D items (e.g. 'has a curved edge or surface / has none').
Say the rule aloud ('all of these have a curved surface') and check: does EVERY shape in this group follow my rule?
Now scatter the SAME shapes and re-sort them by a different property (e.g. 'has a triangular face / has no triangular face'); notice which shapes move to a different hoop and why.
activities.intendedInsight: A sort rests on one geometric property held constant and applied to every item; the same collection can be grouped validly in more than one way depending on which property you choose.

activities.title: Guess my rule
feedback: If a child cannot state a single rule that every group member satisfies, model one aloud ('these all have a triangular face') and check each member against it.

If the inferred rule is a non-geometric feature such as colour or size, point to two members of the SAME group that differ in that named feature (e.g. two different colours) yet were grouped together, so the child sees appearance cannot be the rule and looks for the shared geometric property.
Confirm success when the child's continuation placements all satisfy the same stated property.
activities.rationale: Inferring someone else's rule separates a child who reads shapes by property from one who grouped by holistic resemblance; it makes the criterion explicit rather than letting it drift.

activities.intendedInsight: Making the hidden criterion explicit forces attention onto defining properties and shows that a good sort rests on one rule every member satisfies.

constraints: The skill is doing: placing shapes, testing a criterion, and re-sorting. A view-only tap-to-reveal illustration does not let the child perform or switch a sort, so it does not build the procedure on its own.

A fixed, scored categorization (sort by a GIVEN rule) can check sorting against a supplied criterion, but because the rule is provided it does not require the child to choose, articulate or switch the criterion; use it to check rather than to build the flexible re-sort.
Insist the rule is a geometric property; when a child groups by colour or size, restrict the set to one colour/size so appearance cannot be the criterion.
Require a SECOND, different sort of the same collection plus a 'guess my rule' inference — these are what best separate property-based sorting from grouping by overall look.

Paper or card cut-outs and real solids have slight thickness and can be held and turned; treat them as physical representations of the mathematical shapes, and ask children about the shape REPRESENTED, not whether the object can be picked up. A rotatable on-screen solid is a model that may supplement, not replace, handling where handling is available.

When naming a specific solid in an example, make sure it fits the property claimed (e.g. use a triangular prism/pyramid when illustrating 'has a triangular face', and only call a solid a cube when it is cube-shaped); do not assume a generic box is a cube.

An optional on-screen drag-into-two-loops sorter with a swappable rule tile and immediate feedback (a shape springing back with a red outline when it breaks the rule) can make the mechanism concrete; this is one possible interaction, not a required one, and its benefit over physical sorting is untested.

pedagogy.summary: At age 9-10 pupils identify 3-D shapes — cubes and other cuboids, prisms, pyramids — from 2-D representations: nets, isometric drawings, and other flat pictures. This sits at the demanding interface of 2-D and 3-D: it requires mentally transforming a flat pattern into a closed solid, tracking which faces will meet and which will end up opposite. Research shows the decisive obstacle is that pupils are misled by how a diagram LOOKS — they judge globally ('it looks like a box') rather than reasoning from properties, and this 'look'-driven error persists for years unless taught against. Success depends on coordinating spatial visualisation (mentally folding/rotating) with explicit domain knowledge (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces never share an edge) — neither alone is enough for anything beyond the simplest case. Effective teaching is hands-on first (cut and fold real nets, build with interlocking pieces), then trains a deliberate strategy: fix a base face, rotate the others up, and anticipate where each face lands — checking the net actually closes with no gaps or overlaps.

This one also has six squares — why doesn't it make a cube?

Correctly rejects the five-face net (a face is missing) and the overlapping six-square net (it won't close).

errorPatterns.nextMove: Make domain knowledge explicit (a cube has six square faces; opposite faces don't share an edge) and require mental folding/closure checking rather than a visual judgement

pedagogy.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D↔3-D relationship. It is best taught by having children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, and verify by folding — then check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close (gaps or overlaps) turns errors into structural learning.
bestPractices: Construct-then-fold-to-verify; have the child predict the solid before folding rather than assembling by trial and error.
Start from a base face and add faces in composites; include tabs for assembly so the model closes cleanly.
Check the count: the built solid's faces, edges and vertices should match the target (a triangular prism has 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
Compare several valid nets for the same solid and diagnose why a non-closing net fails — is it the face-set or the arrangement?
keyRepresentations: Card or Polydron nets folded into solids

The triangular-prism net: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles forming a band

commonMisconceptions: Falls back on the familiar cube 'cross' net and cannot generate a net for a different solid.

learn.summary: Building 3-D shapes from nets is a procedural skill that consolidates the 2-D to 3-D relationship. Children construct a net (measure, draw, cut, fold, tape), predict which solid it makes, then fold to verify and check that every face, edge and vertex of the built solid matches the target. Anchoring on a base face and adding faces as composites (e.g. a band of rectangles plus two triangular ends) reduces trial-and-error, and diagnosing why a faulty net won't close — gaps or overlaps — turns errors into structural learning. The worked example throughout is the triangular prism: two congruent triangles plus three rectangles, with 5 faces, 9 edges and 6 vertices.

activities.title: Construct and fold the net of a triangular prism
feedback: Before folding, ask: which rectangle is the base, and how will each face meet its neighbours when folded? A band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end is one reliable layout to start from. Other valid layouts exist, such as one with a rectangle attached to a triangle, so test the fold rather than rejecting a net only because it has no band.

If a triangle is left flapping, or a gap remains even though the pieces were cut accurately, check two things. First, the layout: will each face meet its neighbour when folded? If not, try redrawing from the band-plus-ends composite. Second, the measurements: each triangle side should equal the width of the rectangle it joins, and all rectangles should have the same length. If the net itself is correct but only the cutting or taping is ragged, provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the layout reasoning rather than scissor control.

When counting, prompt: how many corners does each triangular end have? So how many vertices altogether? How many edges are on each triangular end, and how many edges join the two ends? Check the totals against 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices.
If the child reproduces a familiar cube 'cross' net, unfold a real triangular prism to reveal its actual net and contrast the two.
activities.rationale: The procedure ends in a genuinely 3-D solid, so folding the net up and rotating the sealed shape to count faces, edges and vertices is the target skill. Successful builders anchor imaged folding to a base face and known composites; diagnosing why a net won't close moves children from judging by appearance to reasoning about structure.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Using card, a ruler and scissors, draw the net of a triangular prism: two congruent triangles and three rectangles of equal length, each rectangle as wide as the triangle side it joins.
Before cutting, predict and say which shape will be the bottom (base) and which two shapes will cap the ends.
Cut out the net, fold along the edges and tape it shut.
Point to the finished solid and count its faces, edges and vertices (target: 5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).
activities.intendedInsight: A valid net is more than the right set of faces — the faces must be arranged so they fold into a closed solid, and the structure of that solid (faces, edges, vertices) can be read off the built 3-D shape rather than the flat drawing.

activities.title: Drag-to-build a net and predict the fold
feedback: On folding, flag gaps, overlaps and any face left flapping so the child can see exactly where the layout fails.
Immediate close/fail feedback on the fold doubles as a check of the construction procedure.
A flat on-screen view slightly under-sells the real 3-D fold, so confirm the count on a rotatable solid or a physical model.
activities.rationale: A drag-to-build editor with a fold animation and immediate close/fail feedback exercises the construction procedure and lets children test many layouts quickly. It is offered as a supplement to physical construction, not a replacement; a flat screen view represents, rather than replaces, the 3-D fold. Efficacy relative to physical building is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: Successful builders use imaged folding anchored to a base face and known composites (a 'line of four' wraps the cube's sides); the weakest reproduce a memorised prototype net; teacher questioning that maps net shapes/sides/points to faces/edges/vertices moves children from appearance to structure.
learnerActions: Drag two triangles and three rectangles onto a grid to lay out a candidate net.
State which solid you predict it will make and which faces will be the base and the ends.
Fold the layout and watch how the rectangles and triangles move. Check whether every face meets its neighbour so the ends are capped and the prism closes.

If a face is left flapping or a gap or overlap appears, rearrange the faces so they meet correctly, for example by re-anchoring on a band of three rectangles with a triangle on each end, then fold again.
Rotate the sealed solid and tap round it to tally faces, edges and vertices.
activities.intendedInsight: A layout that 'looks fine' flat may still fail to close. Checking how each face will meet its neighbours when folded is what shows whether the prism seals. A band of three rectangles with triangular ends is one dependable layout, but not the only valid one.

activities.title: Compare and diagnose nets for the same solid
feedback: If the child counts wrong faces (e.g. four rectangles, or two triangles and two rectangles), hand them the target prism and match each of its faces to a net shape before deciding; count faces first.

For an arrangement failure, have the child trace which edges will meet when folded and find where faces overlap or leave a gap. Rearranging into a band of three rectangles between the two triangular ends is one reliable fix, though not the only valid net.
A sorting task like this can check and build classification of nets, but it does not itself elicit independent construction of a net from scratch; use it alongside, not instead of, building.
activities.rationale: Comparing valid nets and diagnosing why a non-closing net fails separates face-set errors from arrangement errors and builds the structural scheme. Coordinating spatial visualisation with property-based reasoning is what lets children see past the 'look' of the flat drawing.
sourceClaims: Spatial visualisation and property-based reasoning must be coordinated by domain knowledge to overcome the 'look' of a 2-D representation, which is why some children build by appearance rather than structure.
learnerActions: Given several candidate nets for a triangular prism, sort them into those that will fold shut and those that will not.

For each failing net, say whether the problem is the face-set (wrong shapes, wrong number or mismatched sizes) or the arrangement (correct faces placed so that, when folded, some overlap or leave a gap).
Find two different valid nets for the same prism and explain why both work.
Reason about a near-miss: if a net has three triangles and two rectangles, could it fold into this prism, or into any closed solid at all? Explain using the faces a triangular prism needs.
activities.intendedInsight: Nets fail for two distinct reasons — the wrong set of faces, or a correct set arranged so it cannot close — and the same solid can have more than one valid net.

constraints: A static exploded or net diagram (even one tagged face-to-face, or where tapping a net face shows where it lands on the solid) is a useful planning reference but does not enact the fold-and-check procedure; use it to support planning, not as the build itself.
Matching or sequencing tasks that pair solids to nets and counts check recognition of nets and counts but do not elicit independent construction of a net; use them as a post-check.
Discussion can prompt a prediction for the child to justify, but talking does not itself elicit the physical construction and folding that is the target skill.
When cutting, folding or taping leaves ragged gaps, the fold-check becomes inconclusive — provide a pre-scored, tabbed template so the check tests the reasoning rather than scissor control.
A flat 2-D interactive represents the 3-D fold and may under-sell it; confirm face/edge/vertex counts on a rotatable or physical solid.
Include assembly tabs so the model closes cleanly.

reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of the triangular prism: 2 triangular faces + 3 rectangular faces = 5 faces; 3 edges on each triangular end (6) + 3 connecting edges = 9 edges; 3 vertices on each triangular end = 6 vertices. These match the source values (5 faces, 9 edges, 6 vertices).

The near-miss prompt (three triangles and two rectangles) is retained as a reasoning probe: that face-set does not form a triangular prism, so the expected answer is 'no'. Kept as a diagnostic question, not as a construction instruction.

The legacy row ranked a 3-D interactive as 'ideal' and a conversation as 'poor'. Comparative efficacy/necessity is not established by the cited sources, so artefacts are presented as options with stated affordances and limits rather than universal claims.

The National Curriculum claim was removed from Activity 1's sourceClaims because that activity's rationale concerns a teaching principle (imaged folding/structure) rather than the curriculum objective itself; the curriculum requirement is retained as a constraint and in the audit.
